title: The Gate at Ginling
subtitle: The fall of Nanjing and the Nanjing Massacre, December 1937 – early 1938
intro: In the autumn of 1937 the Japanese army fought its way up the Yangtze from Shanghai toward Nanjing, the capital of Nationalist China. The government left. Most foreigners left. A small group of about twenty Americans and Europeans, among them missionaries, teachers, doctors and a German businessman, stayed behind with Chinese colleagues. Late in November they set up a 'Safety Zone' of about four square kilometres in the western part of the city, hoping both armies would leave it alone. The city fell on 13 December. For the next six weeks or more, Japanese soldiers killed, looted, burned and raped across the city and the surrounding countryside, on a scale that the people inside the Zone could only partly measure.

This chapter leaves out graphic detail on purpose. Its subject is what the diarists themselves wrote down: the size of what they saw, their fear, the long days at gates and in hospital wards, the arguments over food and flags and registration, and how they judged themselves. Minnie Vautrin, an American, and Cheng Ruifang, a Chinese dormitory matron, kept separate diaries at the same women's college on the same nights. They give us two views of one gate. John Rabe was a Siemens manager and a member of the Nazi Party. He used his swastika armband to turn soldiers out of his garden, and wrote to Hitler hoping he would help. The surgeons, professors and clergy around him wrote letters that went out in pieces, by gunboat or sewn into coat linings.

Japanese records sit on the other side of the same days, and they are harder to read. A divisional commander noted the policy toward prisoners in his diary on the day the city fell. The theatre commander rode in at the head of a victory parade and wrote in his field diary. Rank-and-file soldiers of the 65th Infantry Regiment recorded the mass killing of prisoners near Mufushan, in diaries a factory worker named Ono Kenji gathered decades later. Back home, newspaper readers followed a 'contest' between two lieutenants that was reported like a sports score. It was printed as journalism, not kept as a diary, and it shows what Japanese readers were being told while the Zone's foreigners were writing protest letters.

Many of these documents had to be fought over afterwards. Rabe's diary was not made public until December 1996. Matsui's diary was published in 1985 in an edition that critics found had been altered. Azuma Shirō's published diary led to a libel suit he lost at Japan's Supreme Court. Questions about how authentic the sources are, and how they should be read, belong to this event's history. Each entry below says how far it can be trusted.

When these diaries are set side by side, the same week comes out very differently in each. To one writer it was a paperwork problem, to another a triumph, and to a third an emergency of the conscience. The record is uneven: it is mostly missionary letters for the first weeks, with few Chinese voices and fewer Japanese ones. That unevenness is part of what the reader should see.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian. Japanese military diaries and newspapers of the period also used the imperial era name: 1937 is Shōwa 12 and 1938 is Shōwa 13. Month and day are the same in both systems, so no conversion is needed. Chinese diarists such as Cheng Ruifang used the Gregorian calendar (Republic of China year 26 = 1937).

eyes.name: Wilhelmina "Minnie" Vautrin
eyes.role: American missionary educator, aged 51; acting head of Ginling College (Jinling Women's College) after most faculty evacuated
eyes.where: Ginling College campus, inside the Safety Zone
eyes.vantage_label: guarding the gate of a women's refugee camp
eyes.authenticity: Typescript diary 1937–1940 in Yale Divinity School Library Special Collections (RG 8 & 11; microfilm Ms 62). Edited by Suping Lu as Terror in Minnie Vautrin's Nanjing (Univ. of Illinois Press, 2008), and paired with Cheng Ruifang's diary in The Undaunted Women of Nanking (SIU Press, 2010). Undisputed.
eyes.bio: Vautrin was born in Secor, Illinois, and had headed the education department at Ginling since 1916. When the city fell she turned the campus into a refuge for women and children. It was built for a few hundred students and held up to about 10,000 people. She spent her days at the front gate and her evenings at the Japanese embassy asking for guards. The strain broke her health. She left China in May 1940 and took her own life in Indianapolis on 14 May 1941.

sources.title: Yale Divinity Library, Nanking Massacre Project: Minnie Vautrin
Excerpts from the Diaries of Minnie Vautrin and Tsen Shui-fang (teaching PDF, American University)
Terror in Minnie Vautrin's Nanjing (University of Illinois Press)
Wikipedia: Minnie Vautrin

eyes.name: Cheng Ruifang (Tsen Shui-fang), née Yue
eyes.role: Chinese nurse and dormitory supervisor (housemother) at Ginling since 1924, aged 62; one of a three-person emergency committee with Vautrin and Chen Feiran
eyes.where: Ginling College campus, inside the Safety Zone
eyes.vantage_label: Chinese staff inside the women's camp
eyes.authenticity: Kept secretly from 8 Dec 1937 to 1 Mar 1938. The manuscript is held by the Second Historical Archives of China, Nanjing. It is widely described as the first known daily diary of the massacre by a Chinese citizen. It was added to UNESCO's Memory of the World register in 2015 as part of the Nanjing Massacre documents. Her written statement was accepted at the Tokyo tribunal as prosecution exhibit 308. The English translation appears in The Undaunted Women of Nanking (2010).
eyes.bio: Cheng was a grandmother in her sixties from Wuchang. She wrote on the same days as Vautrin and in the same buildings, but as a Chinese woman who could be taken herself. Her refugee counts often run higher than Vautrin's. She notes births and deaths in the camp and the friction between hungry refugees and the staff. She also notices Vautrin's exhaustion, which Vautrin's own diary hides.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Tsen Shui Fang
Global Times feature on Cheng Ruifang's diary and tribunal testimony (2026)
Excerpts from the Diaries of Minnie Vautrin and Tsen Shui-fang

eyes.name: John Rabe
eyes.role: Siemens China manager in Nanjing, aged 55; local Nazi Party group leader; chairman of the International Committee for the Nanking Safety Zone
eyes.where: His house and compound on Xiaofenqiao, inside the Safety Zone, sheltering about 600 refugees
eyes.vantage_label: chairman of the Zone, a Nazi among the missionaries
eyes.authenticity: Typed diary of about 2,117 pages in eight volumes, kept by his family. It was made public in New York in December 1996 with help from Iris Chang and his granddaughter Ursula Reinhardt. It was edited by Erwin Wickert as Der gute Deutsche von Nanking (1997) and published in English as The Good Man of Nanking (Knopf, 1998). Scholars accept it as authentic because it matches the missionary records. The diary includes pasted-in copies of Committee letters.
eyes.bio: Rabe was a Hamburg merchant who had lived in China for decades. He stayed to protect his Chinese employees and ended up leading the whole Zone. His Party armband and the swastika flag over his garden gave him a kind of authority over Japanese soldiers, since Germany and Japan were partners. He believed Hitler would be appalled. Back in Berlin in 1938 he lectured and wrote to Hitler, and was then detained by the Gestapo and silenced.

sources.title: Wikipedia: John Rabe
Wikipedia: The Good Man of Nanking
CUHK Nanjing Massacre archive: Reuters report on the diary's release, 12 Dec 1996

eyes.name: Dr. Robert O. Wilson
eyes.role: American surgeon at the University of Nanking (Drum Tower) Hospital, aged 33; for weeks effectively the only surgeon in the city
eyes.side: American / Safety Zone, Red Cross committee
eyes.where: University Hospital, inside the Safety Zone
eyes.authenticity: Running 'diary-letters' to his family, held at Yale Divinity Library (RG 11, Box 229: NMP0014 Sept 24–Dec 14 1937; NMP0016 Dec 15 1937–Jan 9 1938; NMP0017 Jan 28–31 1938). He testified at the Tokyo tribunal in July 1946. Undisputed.
eyes.bio: Wilson was born in Nanjing to Methodist missionaries and trained at Princeton and Harvard. He returned in 1936 and chose to stay. His letters come from the receiving end. For six or seven weeks the wounded kept arriving, and he wrote to his family at night after operating all day.

sources.title: Yale Divinity Library: Robert O. Wilson papers (Nanking Massacre Project)
Wikipedia: Robert O. Wilson
Barnard MCT: Wilson letter on bombings before the fall (9 Dec 1937)

eyes.name: George Ashmore Fitch
eyes.role: American YMCA secretary, aged 54; director of the Safety Zone
eyes.vantage_label: administrator of the Zone, later its courier
eyes.authenticity: His diary was copied in Shanghai and circulated in mimeograph in early 1938. Excerpts were published in the US press and quoted in H.J. Timperley's What War Means (1938). Fitch later retold it in his memoir My Eighty Years in China (1967). Parts of the circulated diary went through other people's hands before printing.
eyes.bio: Fitch was born in Suzhou, China, and had run the Nanjing YMCA since 1936. His diary covers the first weeks of the occupation and was among the first accounts to reach the outside world. He left on a Japanese military train in January 1938 with reels of John Magee's 16 mm film sewn into his coat. He then showed the film to officials and audiences across the United States.

sources.title: Wikipedia: George Ashmore Fitch
Biographical Dictionary of Chinese Christianity: Fitch, George Ashmore

eyes.name: Rev. James Henry McCallum
eyes.role: American Disciples of Christ missionary, aged 44; administrator at the University Hospital
eyes.side: American / Safety Zone, Red Cross committee
eyes.authenticity: His diary (Dec 1937–Jan 1938) was written for his family. It was circulated, excerpted in Timperley (1938), and later entered at the Tokyo tribunal. It is undisputed. (His life dates come from standard reference works and were not re-checked online for this chapter.)
eyes.bio: McCallum kept the hospital fed, staffed and supplied while Wilson operated. His diary records the scale of the assaults on women in counts per night. He wrote in anger and in disbelief that the occupiers did not understand what they were doing to themselves.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Nanjing Massacre (quotes McCallum's 19 Dec 1937 entry)

eyes.name: Miner Searle Bates
eyes.role: American history professor at the University of Nanking, aged 40; Safety Zone committee member
eyes.where: University of Nanking campus, inside the Safety Zone
eyes.authenticity: His running letters to his wife Lilliath, Dec 24 1937 to Mar 1938, and his notes and protest letters to the Japanese Embassy are at Yale Divinity Library (NMP0034–0054, NMP0109, NMP0145, NMP0162). He testified at the Tokyo tribunal. Undisputed.
eyes.bio: Bates was a trained historian and wrote as one. He kept careful tallies, signed formal protests, and wrote the first summary that the reporters carried out. His letters to his wife move between bare statistics and private confession.

sources.title: Yale Divinity Library: Nanking Massacre Project finding aid (Bates items)

eyes.name: Lewis S. C. Smythe
eyes.role: American sociologist at the University of Nanking, aged 36; Secretary of the Safety Zone International Committee (14 Dec 1937–10 Feb 1938)
eyes.vantage_label: the Committee's letter-writer and later its surveyor
eyes.authenticity: Daily protest letters to the Japanese Embassy (e.g. NMP0156, NMP0171, NMP0173) and family letters are at Yale Divinity Library. His survey War Damage in the Nanking Area (1938) was based on fieldwork in March–April 1938. Undisputed.
eyes.bio: Smythe wrote and numbered the cases. Almost every day he sent the Japanese Embassy lists of incidents in the Zone. In spring 1938 he became the event's first statistician, sending students door to door to count the dead and the losses.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Lewis S. C. Smythe
Yale Divinity Library: Nanking Massacre Project finding aid (Smythe items)

eyes.name: Rev. John Gillespie Magee
eyes.role: American Episcopal priest, aged 53; chairman of the Nanking International Red Cross Committee
eyes.side: American / Red Cross and Safety Zone
eyes.where: Moving through the Zone and hospital with a 16 mm camera
eyes.authenticity: Letters to his wife Faith (Magee Family Papers, Yale Divinity Library) and about eight reels of 16 mm film with his own written narration. Two original massacre-era reels were given to Yale by his grandson and digitised in 2016. Copies were sent to Berlin by Georg Rosen and shown in the US by Fitch. Undisputed.
eyes.bio: Magee was a Pittsburgh-born Yale graduate who had worked in Nanjing since 1912. He filmed wounded refugees in the hospital and the Ginling camp, with Japanese permission to carry a camera. He could not film the worst scenes without being caught. His film is the only moving-picture record made at the time. He later testified at the Tokyo tribunal and served as Episcopal chaplain at Yale.

sources.title: Yale News: Donated film reels contain footage of Nanking Massacre (2016)
The China Project: What atrocity looks like — John Magee's footage
China WW2: The Camera as a Weapon

eyes.name: Georg Rosen
eyes.role: Secretary of the German embassy in Nanjing, aged 42; returned to the city in January 1938
eyes.authenticity: Dated official reports to the German Foreign Ministry, held in the German diplomatic archives (Politisches Archiv). His report of 10 Feb 1938 on Magee's film is widely cited. Undisputed. (Exact return date to Nanjing not re-verified online for this chapter.)
eyes.bio: Rosen was a career diplomat with Jewish ancestry, serving a Nazi state that would soon push him out. He came back to Nanjing in January 1938, after the worst weeks. He wrote to Berlin in plain terms and sent a copy of Magee's film, asking that it be shown to the leadership. It changed nothing.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Nanjing Massacre (quotes Rosen's 10 Feb 1938 report)
China WW2: The Camera as a Weapon (Rosen's copy of the film)

eyes.name: Lieutenant General Nakajima Kesago
eyes.role: Commander of the Japanese 16th Division, aged 56
eyes.side: Imperial Japanese Army, Shanghai Expeditionary Force
eyes.where: Approaching and entering Nanjing from the east (Zhongshan and Taiping gates)
eyes.authenticity: His field diary was concealed for decades. Excerpts were published in Japan in the early 1980s (commonly cited as a 1984 special issue of the magazine Rekishi to Jinbutsu) and in the Kaikōsha collection Nankin senshi shiryōshū. Its genuineness is not seriously contested. Arguments are about interpretation. The content of the 13 Dec entry is summarised here from standard scholarship and was not re-checked online for this chapter.
eyes.bio: Nakajima was a former head of the Kempeitai (military police) and was known as a hard man. His division took the eastern gates and the Purple Mountain sector. Historians cite his diary because it states a policy toward captured soldiers in a senior officer's own hand, on the day the city fell.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Kesago Nakajima
Wikipedia: Nanjing Massacre (notes publication of Nakajima diary excerpts)

eyes.name: General Matsui Iwane
eyes.role: Commander of the Central China Area Army, aged 59
eyes.where: Field headquarters near Suzhou, then Nanjing for the entry ceremony (17 Dec)
eyes.authenticity: His field diary was published in 1985 in an edition edited by the denialist writer Tanaka Masaaki. Japanese researchers, notably Itakura Yoshiaki, later showed that Tanaka had altered several hundred passages. Treat quotations from that edition with caution. Matsui's remarks to aides and diplomats are recorded by others. He was convicted at the Tokyo tribunal of failing to prevent the atrocities and was hanged on 23 Dec 1948.
eyes.bio: Matsui was an elderly, ailing general who thought of himself as a friend of Asian unity. He pushed to take the capital and insisted on a grand entry parade on 17 December. In his diary he played down soldiers' misconduct as partly 'unavoidable'. To people around him he admitted something grievous had happened. He was recalled in February 1938.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Iwane Matsui

eyes.name: Soldiers of the 65th Infantry Regiment (Yamada Detachment), diaries compiled by Ono Kenji
eyes.role: Rank-and-file conscripts and NCOs from Fukushima Prefecture, 13th Division's Yamada Detachment
eyes.where: North of the city along the Yangtze, at Mufushan (Mufu Mountain)
eyes.authenticity: These are about twenty field diaries collected from veterans and their families in the 1980s–90s by Ono Kenji, a chemical-plant worker and amateur historian. They were published in Japanese in the mid-1990s (Nankin daigyakusatsu o kiroku shita kōgun heishitachi, eds. Ono, Fujiwara Akira and Honda Katsuichi). They are many authors, each with his own dated diary, grouped here because they describe the same events. Accepted by mainstream historians. Denialists dispute how they should be read, not whether they exist.
eyes.bio: These men had been farmers and clerks from northern Japan. Their diaries record marching, rain, rations and home. They also record that thousands of prisoners taken at Mufushan were held and then killed at the river over several nights. Ono's work matters because it brings in the ordinary soldier's view, which official histories leave out.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Nanjing Massacre (on Ono Kenji's collection and Mufushan)

eyes.name: Azuma Shirō
eyes.role: Private first class, 20th Infantry Regiment, 16th Division, aged 25
eyes.where: With his platoon in and around Nanjing
eyes.authenticity: DISPUTED. Azuma published material from his wartime diary in 1987 (Waga Nankin puratōn) and the fuller diary in 2001. His former squad leader Hashimoto Mitsuharu sued for libel over one episode. Azuma lost in the Tokyo courts, and in 2000 the Supreme Court rejected his appeal, finding that act as described physically impossible. Critics say parts were rewritten after the war. Supporters say the court ruled only on that one passage. Read his entries as a veteran's contested testimony.
eyes.bio: Azuma came from Kyoto and was among the first Japanese veterans to speak publicly about Nanjing. He did so from the 1980s until his death, and faced threats for it. His case shows how a soldier's diary became a battleground in Japanese memory politics.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Shiro Azuma

eyes.name: Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shimbun / Osaka Mainichi Shimbun (war correspondents Asami Kazuo, Suzuki Jirō and others)
eyes.role: Japanese mass-circulation newspapers and their front-line correspondents
eyes.where: Correspondents with the advancing army; readers across Japan
eyes.vantage_label: the home front, reading the war as news
eyes.authenticity: PRESS, NOT A DIARY. Included to show how the campaign was framed for Japanese readers under censorship. The four 'hundred-man killing contest' articles about Second Lieutenants Mukai Toshiaki and Noda Tsuyoshi ran 30 Nov–13 Dec 1937 and were partly translated in the Japan Advertiser. Historians debate whether the contest itself happened as reported. Both officers were executed after the Nanjing war crimes tribunal on 28 Jan 1948. Their families' defamation suit against later writers and papers failed in 2005 and was finally rejected in 2006.
eyes.bio: These papers do not record what anyone witnessed. They show what the public was offered: the advance as a sporting race, cheering lantern parades, and nothing about what was happening in the Zone. Their tone is the opposite of the protest letters being typed in Nanjing in the same week.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Contest to kill 100 people using a sword
Wikipedia: Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shimbun

entries.headline: A German businessman is made chairman of the Safety Zone
entries.digest: With Shanghai lost and the government preparing to leave, foreign residents meet and form an International Committee for a neutral Safety Zone in western Nanjing. They choose Rabe as chairman, partly because a German Nazi Party member might carry weight with Japan, Germany's partner. He accepts and starts lobbying both armies.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: John Rabe; Wikipedia: Nanking Safety Zone (committee formally established 22 Nov 1937).

entries.headline: A 'killing contest' between two lieutenants is reported like a race
entries.digest: The first of four articles describes two second lieutenants competing to be first to cut down a hundred men with the sword on the road to Nanjing. It is written as a light, heroic human-interest story with a running tally. Japanese readers get the advance as entertainment, while the Zone committee in Nanjing is still mapping its boundaries.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: Contest to kill 100 people using a sword; Wikipedia: Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shimbun (four articles 30 Nov–13 Dec 1937). Exact dates of the 2nd and 3rd articles not confirmed.

entries.headline: The mayor hands the Zone to the foreigners and leaves
entries.digest: Mayor Ma Chaojun orders the remaining Chinese residents into the Safety Zone and passes administration of it to Rabe's committee, with some rice, flour and cash. Then he goes. The foreigners have become caretakers of a crowded quarter of the capital, with no police and no promise from the Japanese side.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: John Rabe; Wikipedia: Nanking Safety Zone (jurisdiction transferred 1 Dec 1937).

entries.headline: Flags go up and the first refugees arrive
entries.digest: Vautrin's staff rehearse the reception plan, with students and workers assigned to direct local families and newcomers to separate buildings. The Safety Zone flags are raised over the campus. That evening the first refugees come through the gate, saying the Chinese military has ordered them out of their homes outside the walls.
entries.source_note: Vautrin diary, 8 Dec 1937, in 'Excerpts from the Diaries of Minnie Vautrin and Tsen Shui-fang' (American Univ. PDF).

entries.headline: A housemother begins a secret diary
entries.digest: Cheng Ruifang starts the diary she will keep until 1 March 1938. She was sixty-two, with every reason to flee, and stayed to run the dormitories and the health unit of what would become the Zone's women's camp. From the first page she records events from inside the Chinese staff, whose own families are also at risk.
entries.source_note: Global Times (2026) feature: diary runs 8 Dec 1937 – 1 Mar 1938; Wikipedia: Tsen Shui Fang.

entries.headline: A surgeon reads the casualties as a countdown
entries.digest: Wilson writes home that the bombing and shelling have filled his wards with civilians. He reads the number and kind of wounds as a sign that the city will fall within days. He has decided to stay and keep operating, though the American embassy staff have moved to the gunboat Panay.
entries.source_note: Wilson letter dated 9 Dec 1937, Yale Divinity Library (Barnard MCT item 636).

entries.headline: Planning for a few thousand, asked for ten
entries.digest: In a letter to the American embassy, now evacuated to the gunboat Panay, Vautrin describes the gunfire close to the walls. She sets out the campus housing plan, which has room for about 2,750, while the Zone committee wants Ginling to take roughly 10,000. She adds that she has had no time to copy out her diary and will do it later.
entries.source_note: Vautrin letter, 9 Dec 1937, Barnard MCT 'Memories of the Nanjing Massacre' item 825.

entries.headline: A last ceasefire bid fails; the defenders break
entries.digest: General Tang Shengzhi, the Chinese defence commander, asks Rabe and his colleague Eduard Sperling to arrange a short truce so his army can withdraw. There is not enough time, and Tang leaves across the Yangtze that evening. Many units never get the order to retreat. Rabe packs bandages and photographs of his grandchildren and waits.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: Battle of Nanjing (Tang's ceasefire bid via Rabe and Sperling, 12 Dec); The Nanjinger article on Rabe (12 Dec preparations).

entries.headline: A city strangely silent, and cut off
entries.digest: After days of bombing and shelling the city goes quiet, and Vautrin finds the silence more frightening than the noise. There is no electricity, water, telephone, telegraph, newspaper or radio. Everyone on campus is waiting to see how the victorious army will behave.
entries.source_note: Vautrin diary, 13 Dec 1937, as quoted in 'Minnie Vautrin: Staring Down Death' (The Mudroom). Phrase is her own, widely quoted.

entries.headline: The first day of occupation: bodies on every block
entries.digest: Rabe drives through the city and finds bodies every hundred or two hundred yards, many of them civilians. He sees soldiers looting shops. At home he orders intruders out of his yard, where about 600 refugees are sheltering, and goes next door to stop an assault. His notes for this day are still mostly about logistics, and they break off in disbelief.
entries.source_note: Rabe diary 13 Dec 1937 as summarised in Wikipedia: The Good Man of Nanking and Wikipedia: Nanjing Massacre; The Nanjinger (600 refugees).

entries.headline: A general writes down the prisoner policy
entries.digest: On the day his division breaks in, Nakajima notes in his diary that, as general policy, the army is not taking prisoners. He records that large groups of surrendering Chinese soldiers are being 'disposed of', and he grumbles about the logistics. Historians cite this entry as evidence that killing captives was intended from the top, not just the work of rogue units.
entries.source_note: Diary excerpts published early 1980s (Rekishi to Jinbutsu special issue, 1984; Kaikōsha Nankin senshi shiryōshū). Day and gist from standard scholarship; not re-verified online this session.

entries.headline: 'Super record': the contest score printed on capture day
entries.digest: On the morning Nanjing falls, the paper reports that both lieutenants have passed a hundred and nobody can tell who got there first. So, it says, they have agreed to go on to 150. Lantern parades celebrating the capture follow across Japan. Nothing about what is happening inside the walls reaches these readers.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shimbun (13 Dec headline; reporters Asami Kazuo and Suzuki Jirō); Wikipedia: Battle of Nanjing (lantern parades, censorship).

entries.headline: Thanking the army for sparing the Zone, then counting
entries.digest: Rabe signs a polite letter to the Japanese commander, thanking him because the Zone was not shelled. On the same day he records the scale of destruction and men shot from behind. He is still being correct while fearing the worst, and the courtesy will not survive the week.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: The Good Man of Nanking (14 Dec thank-you letter); CUHK Reuters report (14 Dec entry on destruction).

entries.headline: Looting next door; nobody can find the commander
entries.digest: Vautrin records a night of artillery and rifle fire and looting in the neighbourhood. The Zone headquarters cannot get through to any Japanese commander. An American reporter who tried to drive out of the city was turned back.
entries.source_note: Vautrin diary, 14 Dec 1937 (American Univ. excerpts PDF).

entries.headline: Soldiers climb the fence; four or five thousand inside
entries.digest: Cheng notes more refugees flowing in from other parts of the Zone. Soldiers come over the campus fence and leave again without serious harm. Her estimate of four to five thousand people is already well above what the buildings were meant to hold.
entries.source_note: Tsen Shui-fang diary under 14 Dec 1937 (American Univ. excerpts PDF; her entries follow Vautrin's dates).

entries.headline: All day at the gate, choosing who comes in
entries.digest: Vautrin stands at the front gate from morning to dark, letting in women and children and asking older women to go home if they can. She writes of two days of looting, killing and rape across the city. She fears that about a thousand disarmed Chinese soldiers whom the Committee had hoped to protect have been taken away and killed. A new Japanese commander seems reasonable, and she lets herself hope.
entries.source_note: Vautrin diary, 15 Dec 1937 (Diaries of Note; Univ. of Washington page; American Univ. PDF gives 'more than 3,000' that night).

entries.headline: Awake all night, listening for boots
entries.digest: Cheng does not sleep for fear of soldiers. She writes that they are searching residences on campus and taking valuables. Like Vautrin, she passes on the rumour that a commander has arrived and things may improve, though she sounds less sure of it.
entries.source_note: Tsen Shui-fang diary under 15 Dec 1937 (American Univ. excerpts PDF).

entries.headline: The killing of civilians is 'appalling'
entries.digest: Wilson begins a new running letter home. He describes the wounded who reach his table, among them survivors of a squad of street cleaners shot in their own headquarters. He calls the slaughter of civilians appalling and says he hardly knows where to begin.
entries.source_note: Wilson family letter begun 15 Dec 1937 (Yale NMP0016); excerpted by UNI Center for Holocaust & Genocide Education and Wikipedia: Robert O. Wilson.

entries.headline: A historian's first summary leaves with the reporters
entries.digest: Bates writes up 'Some Pictures from Nanking', a short factual account of the first days of occupation. The handful of foreign correspondents in the city are about to leave by gunboat for Shanghai, and his notes go with them. They help shape the first reports that reach the world.
entries.source_note: Yale Divinity Library finding aid NMP0145, dated 15 Dec 1937; Wikipedia: F. Tillman Durdin (left on USS Oahu, 15 Dec per that article).

entries.headline: A hundred soldiers search for hidden men
entries.digest: More than a hundred Japanese soldiers comb the campus for Chinese soldiers. Afterwards a senior officer gives Vautrin a written statement that only women and children are there. She hears of girls taken from a nearby language school and from homes. She sees a truck of young women pass the gate calling out for someone to save them, and can do nothing. She now counts about 4,000 on campus.
entries.source_note: Vautrin diary, 16 Dec 1937 (American Univ. PDF; The Mudroom; Women's Media Center).

entries.headline: Grey clothing becomes dangerous; people burn it
entries.digest: Cheng records that the searching soldiers treat any grey cloth as proof of a Chinese uniform. Refugees hurry to burn or hide such garments. Her count of seven to eight thousand is nearly double Vautrin's for the same night. They were both counting while overwhelmed, and the gap shows how far beyond counting the camp had grown.
entries.source_note: Tsen Shui-fang diary under 16 Dec 1937 (American Univ. excerpts PDF).

entries.headline: The Committee's secretary starts the paper trail
entries.digest: Smythe, now Secretary of the Committee, writes formally to the Japanese side, to Tokuyasu Fukuda of the embassy. It is the first of a long run of numbered case lists and protests. His method is to put every incident on paper with a name and a place, so that nobody can later say they were not told.
entries.source_note: Yale Divinity Library finding aid NMP0156, Smythe to Fukuda, 16 Dec 1937.

entries.place: Mufushan, on the Yangtze north of the city
entries.headline: Thousands of prisoners, and orders to 'dispose' of them
entries.digest: The regiment's diaries record taking an enormous number of surrendered soldiers and civilians near Mufushan, far too many to feed or guard. Over the next nights the prisoners are marched to the riverbank and killed, and the diarists note it alongside cold, rations and fatigue. Some write uneasily. Others simply log it as the day's work. Historians estimate the victims at many thousands.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: Nanjing Massacre (Mufushan killings 15–17 Dec by Yamada Detachment incl. 65th Regiment; Ono Kenji's diary collection). Individual diary dates not checked.

entries.headline: Lured to the gate while the camp is raided
entries.digest: Soldiers hold Vautrin, Chinese staff and workers at the front gate for questioning and take several people away. It becomes clear later that this was a decoy, and young women were taken from the compound while the staff were pinned at the gate. The American flag is pulled down from the quadrangle and later found dropped near the Science Building. It is the night she cannot forgive herself for.
entries.source_note: Vautrin diary, 17 Dec 1937 (American Univ. PDF; The Nanjinger on the decoy and the twelve girls).

entries.headline: Eleven girls taken; 'could not help but feel heartbroken'
entries.digest: Cheng records the same scene at the gate and puts the number of girls taken that night at eleven. She writes that she cannot help feeling heartbroken. Some of those detained, including her colleague Chen Feiran, are later let go. New refugees keep arriving all the same, because nowhere else feels safer.
entries.source_note: Cheng Ruifang diary, 17 Dec 1937, per Global Times (2026) and American Univ. PDF.

entries.headline: Protest to the embassy: 'restore order among your troops'
entries.digest: Rabe writes to Kiyoshi Fukui at the Japanese embassy asking that order be restored among the troops. That night he records reports of up to a thousand women and girls assaulted in the city, about a hundred of them at Ginling. His tone has changed from grateful chairman to angry witness.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: The Good Man of Nanking and Wikipedia: Nanjing Massacre (17 Dec letter and entry); McLean County Museum article (Ginling figure).

entries.headline: The commander rides in at the head of a parade
entries.digest: Matsui enters the city on horseback at the head of a formal victory parade, on the date he had insisted on. The streets along the route had been cleared for the ceremony. His diary treats the day as a triumph. At Ginling that same evening, Vautrin and Cheng are recording the raid at the gate.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: Iwane Matsui (victory parade 17 Dec, the date he insisted on). Diary wording itself not checked; 1985 edition altered (see authenticity).

entries.headline: Proclamations for the gate, which soldiers ignore
entries.digest: Vautrin goes to the American and Japanese embassies to report what happened and comes back with letters and proclamations to post on the gates. She estimates about 5,000 on campus. In the weeks that follow, soldiers often tear the notices down. She keeps going back for new ones.
entries.source_note: Vautrin diary, 18 Dec 1937 (American Univ. PDF); Wikipedia: Minnie Vautrin (repeated embassy trips 18 Dec–13 Jan).

entries.headline: Most of the girls come back; two military police arrive
entries.digest: Cheng records with relief that most of the girls taken the night before have been released. Her count is now over 9,000. After Vautrin's written protest the Japanese consul sends two military policemen for the night, which is a token gesture for a camp this size.
entries.source_note: Tsen Shui-fang diary under 18 Dec 1937 (American Univ. excerpts PDF).

entries.place: University Hospital and University Middle School
entries.headline: Ten intrusions in one night at a school of 8,000
entries.digest: Continuing his letter, Wilson describes the University Middle School, where about 8,000 refugees are packed in. Soldiers came in about ten times in a single night, taking food and bedding and assaulting women. He writes of a wounded eight-year-old boy he expects to pull through, and of the families of his own Chinese colleagues.
entries.source_note: Wilson family letter, 18 Dec 1937 section (Yale NMP0016); summarised by UNI CHGE and AwesomeStories.

entries.headline: After the memorial service, an admission to an aide
entries.digest: A day after the parade, Matsui is reported as telling a civilian aide that he now realises the army has done grievous harm to the city without meaning to. The remark was recorded by people around him, not in the published diary, which plays down misconduct. The gap between the two records is part of his story.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: Nanjing Massacre (Matsui's 18 Dec remark to a civilian aide). Source is a reported statement, not his diary.

entries.headline: A torch, an armband, and six men retreat over the wall
entries.digest: At night Rabe finds six soldiers who have climbed his garden wall and are trying to open the gates from inside. He shines a torch on them and holds up his swastika armband, and they go back over the wall when he orders them out. He is aware of the irony, and he relies on it every night.
entries.source_note: Rabe diary, 19 Dec 1937, Woods trans. p. 82, as quoted on Univ. of Washington 'johnrabe' page.

entries.headline: A hospital administrator counts assaults by the thousand
entries.digest: McCallum writes in his diary that the foreigners now estimate about a thousand assaults on women a night, and many by day. He describes being unable to be everywhere, and the hospital filling with the results. Like Vautrin on this day, he writes in fury.
entries.source_note: McCallum diary, 19 Dec 1937, quoted in Wikipedia: Nanjing Massacre.

entries.headline: Rice runs short; fires on the skyline
entries.digest: With thousands to feed, Vautrin gets a letter allowing her to draw rice from the Zone office. Four gendarmes are posted on campus. From the grounds she watches fires burning in several districts as soldiers burn the looted shops.
entries.source_note: Vautrin diary, 19 Dec 1937 (American Univ. PDF); Wikipedia: Minnie Vautrin notes her fury in this entry.

entries.headline: Eight raids in a day; should married women go home?
entries.digest: Cheng counts about eight separate visits by soldiers in one day. Staff and the foreigners argue over whether to send married women home to make room and lower the risk for the young. She records the argument without settling it.
entries.source_note: Tsen Shui-fang diary under 19 Dec 1937 (American Univ. excerpts PDF).

entries.headline: A guard detail she does not trust; three births
entries.digest: Twenty-four soldiers and a sergeant arrive to 'protect' the campus, and Cheng says plainly that she does not trust them. On the same page she notes three babies born in the camp that day and one death. The camp is now a whole town, with births as well as deaths.
entries.source_note: Tsen Shui-fang diary under 20 Dec 1937 (American Univ. excerpts PDF).

entries.headline: Red tickets for rice; ten thousand in the buildings
entries.digest: To stop the crush at the rice kettles, staff start issuing red tags and tickets. Vautrin estimates about 10,000 people on campus. She hears that dozens of electric-plant workers have been killed, the men the occupiers would need to get the lights back on. Someone asks about holding an English Christmas service.
entries.source_note: Vautrin diary, 22 Dec 1937 (American Univ. excerpts PDF).

entries.headline: Registration ordered; a telegram refused
entries.digest: Cheng records that the Japanese authorities now require refugees to register, which everyone understands as a sorting of men who might be soldiers. The consul refuses to send a telegram asking for outside help. Professor Bates raises the idea of a Christmas observance, and she sets it down without comment.
entries.source_note: Tsen Shui-fang diary under 22 Dec 1937 (American Univ. excerpts PDF).

entries.headline: Christmas service cancelled; lights out at 8:30
entries.digest: The planned Christmas service is called off because a gathering could draw soldiers. Meat and fresh food have almost run out, electric light is cut at 8:30 p.m., and it rains. The entry is short and quiet, written by someone very tired.
entries.source_note: Vautrin diary, 23 Dec 1937 (American Univ. excerpts PDF).

entries.headline: Soldiers at the gate asking for firewood
entries.digest: Soldiers come to the gate asking for firewood and food. Fuel is so scarce that staff avoid lighting fires at all. Cheng notes that a colleague, Wei, has still not come back, and the buildings are as crowded as ever.
entries.source_note: Tsen Shui-fang diary under 23 Dec 1937 (American Univ. excerpts PDF).

entries.headline: Christmas Eve among the dead: a witness who will not be silent
entries.digest: Rabe writes that he has made himself look at victims, though it is especially hard at Christmas, so that he can testify as an eyewitness rather than pass on hearsay. He says he cannot stay silent about such cruelty. He is already thinking about how to make Berlin believe him.
entries.quote: A man cannot be silent about this kind of cruelty!
entries.source_note: Rabe diary, 24 Dec 1937, Woods trans. p. 92, via Univ. of Washington 'johnrabe' page. Quote is the 1998 English translation (short phrase widely cited); treat as translation.

entries.headline: Ten days of looting and burning, and helplessness
entries.digest: Fitch looks back over roughly ten days of looting, burning and killing. He writes of watching it while being almost powerless to stop it, which he finds a kind of torment of its own. He says he hardly knows where to start, but he means to write it all down for anyone who will read it.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: George Ashmore Fitch (24 Dec 1937 diary entry).

entries.headline: A bargain at the registration, and its cost
entries.digest: During the registration, Japanese officers demand women from the camp. Vautrin lets them take a group of women identified as former prostitutes, after the officers promise to leave the others alone. It is a bargain made under pressure, and her own diary shows how much it troubled her conscience.
entries.source_note: Vautrin diary, 24 Dec 1937, as reported in China Daily (Pacific Atrocities Education PDF): 21 women released on that promise.

entries.headline: Christmas Eve notes and a letter to his wife
entries.digest: Bates starts the long run of letters to Lilliath that he will keep up into March. On the same day he puts together his notes on December. In the letters he can admit to the despair that his formal protests to the embassy leave out.
entries.source_note: Yale Divinity Library finding aid NMP0034 (letter 24 Dec 1937) and NMP0109 ('Notes by Bates during December 1937', Christmas Eve).

entries.headline: Christmas Day, another case list to the embassy
entries.digest: On Christmas Day Smythe sends the Japanese embassy another letter with a further batch of numbered incidents. He writes again the next day. The routine is part of the protest: the foreigners keep recording, so the embassy cannot claim it did not know.
entries.source_note: Yale Divinity Library finding aid NMP0171 (25 Dec 1937) and NMP0173 (26 Dec 1937).

entries.headline: A priest writes to his wife; a camera keeps rolling
entries.digest: In a December letter to his wife Faith, Magee sums up the first week of occupation as one of murder and rape on a scale he could hardly put into words. Through December and January he films wounded patients at the hospital and the women's camp at Ginling, with Vautrin on screen. He films carefully, because being caught would cost him the camera.
entries.source_note: Yale News (2016): Dec 1937 letter to his wife; reel one shows Ginling and Vautrin. China WW2: filming conditions. Exact date of letter not confirmed.

entries.headline: A private's diary, later fought over in court
entries.digest: Azuma's wartime diary follows his platoon into the city and through the occupation. It records looting, the treatment of prisoners and civilians, and the soldiers' casual contempt for Chinese people. He later said he had shared that contempt. One episode in it, attributed to his squad leader, became the subject of a libel suit that the Japanese courts decided against him.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: Shiro Azuma (diary, 1987 & 2001 publications, libel suit, 2000 Supreme Court ruling). Individual entry dates not checked; disputed.

entries.headline: A New Year toast and a confession
entries.digest: At a New Year gathering Matsui tells a Japanese diplomat that his men have done something very wrong and deeply regrettable. Like the 18 December remark, this is recorded by someone else. His diary edition does not show this candour, and his trial in 1948 turned partly on the gap.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: Nanjing Massacre (New Year's Day remark to a Japanese diplomat).

entries.headline: Sunlight, and three visitors she cannot speak to
entries.digest: A sunny day lifts spirits a little among people whose homes have been burned or looted. Three elderly Japanese women from a patriotic women's defence association visit during the rice distribution and look around without saying much. Vautrin wishes she could speak Japanese and tell them what the refugees have been through.
entries.source_note: Vautrin diary, 2 Jan 1938, via Univ. of Washington 'minnievautrin' page.

entries.headline: Planning trades for widows; a caretaker's son still missing
entries.digest: Writing to colleagues in Shanghai, Vautrin reports a meeting of camp heads, a military-police guard at the gate, and the looting of college property. A caretaker's son taken in December has never come back. She is already thinking about the future and asks for industrial training so that widowed women can support their children.
entries.source_note: Vautrin letter, 11 Jan 1938, Barnard MCT item 825.

entries.headline: Film sewn into a coat lining
entries.digest: Fitch arranges to be called to Shanghai on official business and leaves on a Japanese military train. Reels of Magee's 16 mm negative are sewn into his camel-hair coat. In Shanghai his diary is copied and passed around, the first full account from the capital since the city was cut off.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: George Ashmore Fitch gives 23 Jan 1938 for a group departure by train; other accounts give late January. BDCC (Fitch memoir) on Shanghai reception.

entries.headline: Still rescuing, six weeks in
entries.digest: Weeks after the fall, Rabe is still being called out to pull a woman away from a soldier. His entries are getting more tired. The Japanese authorities are pushing refugees out of the Zone and back to wrecked homes, and the danger is less than in December but has not ended.
entries.source_note: CUHK archive Reuters report, 12 Dec 1996 (cites 30 Jan 1938 entry); Wikipedia: Nanking Safety Zone (28 Jan evacuation order).

entries.headline: Deadline day: the other camps empty, Ginling fills
entries.digest: The Japanese deadline for refugees to leave the camps and go home arrives. Women and children from other camps who are too afraid to go home come to Ginling instead. Vautrin keeps the gate open, so the order to disperse ends up filling her campus again.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: Minnie Vautrin (4 Feb 1938); Wikipedia: Nanking Safety Zone (4 Feb deadline).

entries.headline: A diplomat sends Magee's film to Berlin
entries.digest: Rosen reports to the Foreign Ministry that Magee's film is plain evidence of what happened. He sends a copy and a shot list, asking that it be shown to the leadership, and wonders openly whether the Japanese high command can restore discipline. Nothing comes of it in Berlin.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: Nanjing Massacre (Rosen's 10 Feb 1938 report); China WW2 'Camera as a Weapon' (copy sent to Berlin).

entries.headline: A warning about what he says in Shanghai
entries.digest: Rabe records a pointed warning from the embassy's Fukui about how he should speak once he reaches Shanghai, a hint that criticism will be noticed. He is getting ready to leave and takes the warning seriously. He decides to save his testimony for Germany.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: The Good Man of Nanking (10 Feb entry, Fukui's threat; year implied 1938).

entries.headline: Told he is being replaced
entries.digest: Matsui learns he will be relieved and replaced by General Hata Shunroku. He leaves Shanghai on 21 February. In Tokyo he is honoured, not disgraced. The reckoning comes ten years later at the international tribunal.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: Iwane Matsui (informed 10 Feb 1938; left Shanghai 21 Feb).

entries.headline: The Safety Zone is renamed out of existence
entries.digest: Under Japanese pressure the International Committee for the Nanking Safety Zone becomes the Nanking International Relief Committee. The Zone as a protected area effectively ends. Smythe's term as secretary has just closed. The foreigners carry on with relief work but give up the claim to a neutral quarter.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: Nanking Safety Zone and Wikipedia: Nanjing Massacre (18 Feb 1938 renaming); Wikipedia: Lewis S. C. Smythe (secretary to 10 Feb).

entries.headline: Rabe leaves, carrying his diary and evidence
entries.digest: Rabe leaves Nanjing for Shanghai with his diaries, documents and a copy of Magee's film. Refugees see him off. In Berlin from April he lectures, sends a report to Hitler, is arrested by the Gestapo, and is released only on condition that he stays silent.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: John Rabe and Wikipedia: Nanking Safety Zone (departure 23 Feb 1938; Berlin 15 Apr; Gestapo).

entries.headline: The housemother's diary falls silent
entries.digest: Cheng's diary ends with the camp still full and the city still occupied. She stays at Ginling. Years later she is too ill to travel to Tokyo, and her sworn written statement goes to the tribunal instead.
entries.source_note: Global Times (2026): diary runs to 1 Mar 1938; tribunal exhibit No. 308.

entries.headline: A surgeon's 'conservative estimate' of the dead
entries.digest: With the worst weeks over, Wilson tries to estimate the toll in a letter. His conservative figure for people killed in cold blood is around 100,000. It is a guess from the operating table and conversations with colleagues, not a count, and he presents it as such.
entries.source_note: Wilson letter, 7 Mar 1938, quoted in Wikipedia: Nanjing Massacre.

entries.headline: Students go door to door counting the dead
entries.digest: Smythe organises a sample survey of households in the city and the countryside. It finds about 12,000 civilians killed within the walls and over 26,000 in the surrounding counties, most of them men taken in sweeps, along with wide destruction of homes and crops. Later historians think it undercounts, because it was a sample of survivors in a city still under occupation.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: Nanjing Massacre (Smythe survey Mar–Apr 1938; Kasahara's view); Yale finding aid NMP0249 (War damage in the Nanjing area).

entries.headline: A census of the camp: 3,310 remain
entries.digest: A mid-March census of the camp counts 3,310 refugees, a third of the December peak. Vautrin's diary moves from rescue to rebuilding, with craft classes and schooling for widows and girls who have nowhere to go. The danger is less constant now, and she spends more of the diary on plans than on alarms.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: Minnie Vautrin (mid-March 1938 census of 3,310).

entries.headline: One year on, reliving it hour by hour
entries.digest: On the first anniversary of the fall, Vautrin writes that the memories are so close she is living through the days again hour by hour. Nothing outward is happening, and the entry is about memory. It is an early sign of the collapse that sent her home in 1940.
entries.source_note: The Nanjinger article on Vautrin's diary (one-year anniversary, Dec 1938). Exact day not confirmed.

convergences.label: Nanjing falls
convergences.note: Four views of one day. Vautrin hears the silence and fears what comes next. Rabe drives past bodies and turns intruders out of his yard. Nakajima notes a no-prisoners policy as an administrative matter. Tokyo readers get a 'super record' in a killing race. Only the first two were trying to find out what was really happening.

convergences.label: The reporters leave; the gate opens wide
convergences.note: On the day the last foreign correspondents leave by gunboat, the Ginling pair stand at the same gate. Vautrin writes about crowd control and hopes for a reasonable commander. Cheng writes about lying awake and soldiers in the dormitories. Wilson starts his letter from the operating room. Bates writes the summary the reporters take out.

convergences.label: Searches for 'soldiers'; the Mufushan prisoners
convergences.note: Inside the Zone, the search for hidden soldiers turns grey clothing into a death sentence, and Smythe begins his numbered protests. Outside the walls, the 65th Regiment's diarists record holding thousands of prisoners. Vautrin and Cheng give very different counts for the same campus that night, about 4,000 against 7,000–8,000.

convergences.label: The victory parade and the raid at the gate
convergences.note: The book's sharpest overlap. Matsui rides in at the head of a triumphal parade. A few kilometres away, Vautrin and Cheng are held at their own gate while young women are taken. Vautrin counts twelve and Cheng eleven, and Cheng's word for how she felt is heartbroken. Rabe writes his first angry protest to the embassy.

convergences.label: Morning after: protests and an admission
convergences.note: The women go to the embassies and bring back proclamations and two military policemen. Wilson describes a school intruded on ten times in one night. Matsui privately admits to an aide that grievous harm has been done. All four recognise the same disaster, but only some of them could do anything about it.

convergences.label: The worst week, counted
convergences.note: Rabe stops intruders with a torch and an armband. McCallum puts the night's assaults in the thousands. Vautrin writes of rice and fires, and Cheng of eight raids in a day. Each of them counts what they can, and none can count all of it.

convergences.label: Christmas Eve in an occupied city
convergences.note: The Christian foreigners each mark the holiday differently. Rabe makes himself look at victims so he can bear witness. Fitch writes about helplessness. Bates begins writing to his wife. Vautrin makes a bargain at the registration that troubled her conscience. The Christmas service had already been cancelled for safety.

convergences.label: Reports to Berlin, warnings in Nanjing, a recall in Shanghai
convergences.note: On one day the German diplomat sends film evidence to a government that will ignore it, the German businessman is warned to be careful what he says, and the Japanese commander learns he is being replaced. This was the moment the outside world could have acted, and none of the three got a response.

ties.note: They ran the Ginling camp together as two of a three-person emergency committee, and their diaries cover the same nights from American and Chinese viewpoints. The two diaries were published together in 2010.
Rabe was chairman of the Safety Zone committee and Smythe its secretary. Many of the letters pasted into Rabe's diary were drafted by Smythe.
Fitch carried Magee's film out of Nanjing sewn into his coat and showed it across the United States without naming the man who shot it.
Rosen sent a copy of Magee's film to the German Foreign Ministry with a report of 10 Feb 1938.
Vautrin and the Ginling camp appear on Magee's first reel. Both sat on the Nanking International Red Cross Committee.
They ran the University Hospital together, Wilson as surgeon and McCallum as administrator, and their accounts back each other up.
Rabe's committee wrote repeatedly to Matsui's army, through its embassy, about soldiers' conduct. Rabe also hoped Hitler would put pressure on Germany's Japanese partner.
Azuma served as a private in Nakajima's 16th Division. They saw the same campaign from the top and the bottom of the division.
The papers celebrated the campaign Matsui commanded, while the army's censorship kept the occupation out of print.
Both were University of Nanking faculty and both later testified at the Tokyo tribunal.
Rabe's 17 Dec entry records reported assaults at Ginling, the campus Vautrin was guarding that same night.

threads_out.note: After Japan's surrender the Tokyo tribunal (1946–48) heard testimony from Wilson, Bates and Magee and accepted Cheng Ruifang's written statement. It convicted Matsui, who was hanged on 23 December 1948. Mukai and Noda were tried and shot in Nanjing in January 1948.

Rabe took his evidence back to Nazi Berlin in April 1938, sent a report to Hitler, and was detained by the Gestapo. Rosen, a German diplomat of Jewish descent, was soon pushed out of the Foreign Service. Germany's alliance with Japan went ahead regardless.

The diaries became evidence in later memory wars: Rabe's was made public in 1996, Matsui's was published in an altered edition in 1985, Azuma's led to a libel suit, and the 'contest' reports produced their own suit decided in 2006. UNESCO added the Nanjing Massacre documents to its Memory of the World register in 2015.
